item.title: Novel computational workflow for selecting virtual patient cohorts for in silico clinical trials
item.description: Objectives: In silico clinical trials are a well-accepted model-informed drug development (MIDD) tool to understand, optimize and predict the effect of drugs across diverse populations [1,2]. Generation and selection of virtual patients for simulating in silico trials remains an open area of research not least due to challenges of selecting virtual patients that are representative of the underlying physiological and clinical characteristics of individual subjects enrolled into clinical trials [3]. While virtual patients can be obtained by sampling sets of parameters from a calibrated non-linear mixed effects model, these may however generate biomarkers outside the expected range of observations, thus impacting the accuracy of in silico clinical trials predictions. To obtain a more representative virtual population, different algorithms can be applied to tailor plausible patient cohorts and yield calibrated virtual patients. In this work, we present a new virtual patient selection workflow using a minimal quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model of chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Methods: A QSP model of HBV disease progression incorporating the effect of standard-of-care therapies (peg-interferon and nucleos(t)ide analogues) was used to generate plausible patient cohorts corresponding to the Everest trial [4] (a real-world clinical study exploring how interferon therapy can achieve functional cure in chronically infected patients). To tailor plausible patients to a virtual cohort mimicking baseline characteristics of patients enrolled into the Everest project, we developed a computational algorithm based on a mixed-integer linear programming framework coupled to a multi-objective optimization genetic algorithm. Subsequently, the virtual patient cohort obtained with this algorithm was used to perform in silico clinical trials mirroring the Everest protocol to validate the workflow. Non-linear relationships between baseline characteristics, prognostic biomarkers, and dosing parameters with clinical endpoints were explored using in silico trials. Results: We show that: (1) the HBV QSP model captures longitudinal biomarker data from untreated patients as well as chronically infected subjects receiving standard-of-care therapies, (2) Plausible patients generated with the model capture HBV disease progression, (3) The novel computational workflow efficiently selects virtual patients matching HBsAg and viral load baseline Everest data distributions, (4) In silico trials that mirrored the Everest trial showed quantitative agreement with clinical end-points thus validating the workflow, (5) In silico trials were leveraged to identify and compare optimal dosing regimens and explore mechanistic pathways in responders and non-responders to interferon. Conclusions: This work proposes and validates a novel QSP-based computational workflow for performing in silico trials, generating mechanistic hypotheses, and identifying optimal dosing regimens.Citations: COI: DW, AN, AS, RD are employees of and hold shares in GSK. item.title: G lobal
item.description: For modeling imprecise and indeterminate data for multi-objective decision making, two different methods: neutrosophic multi-objective linear/non-linear programming neutrosophic goal programming, which have been very recently proposed in the literatuire. In many economic problems, the well-known probabilities or fuzzy solutions procedures are not suitable because they cannot deal the situation when indeterminacy inherently involves in the problem. In this case we propose a new concept in optimization problem under uncertainty and indeterminacy. It is an extension of fuzzy and intuitionistic fuzzy optimization in which the degrees of indeterminacy and falsity (rejection) of objectives and constraints are simultaneously considered together with the degrees of truth membership (satisfaction/acceptance). The drawbacks of the existing neutrosophic optimization models have been presented and new framework of multi-objective optimization in neutrosophic environment has been proposed. The essence of the proposed approach is that it is capable of dealing with indeterminacy and falsity simultaneously.

item.title: cuPDQPx: A GPU-Accelerated Restarted Halpern PDHG for Large-Scale Convex Quadratic Programming
item.description: We present cuPDQPx, a GPU-accelerated, factorization-free first-order solver for large-scale convex quadratic programming (QP). Building on the restarted reflected Halpern primal-dual framework of cuPDLPx, we introduce an auxiliary-variable splitting that yields explicit updates without linearizing the quadratic objective or solving inner quadratic subproblems. A preconditioned proximal point interpretation yields both sublinear and linear fixed-point residual convergence guarantees. For practical efficiency, cuPDQPx integrates diagonal preconditioning, step-size selection, adaptive restart, and adaptive primal and quadratic weight updates. cuPDQPx is implemented in C and CUDA with optimized sparse matrix-vector products, kernel fusion, and CUDA Graphs. Numerical experiments on the Maros-Mészáros collection, a convex subset of QPLIB, and synthetic large-scale QPs demonstrate that cuPDQPx has strong numerical performance at both $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-8}$ tolerances.

item.title: On the Convergence of Vanilla Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise and Index Sampling
item.description: Understanding how stochastic gradient noise affects the convergence of Adam is an important problem in stochastic optimization, particularly when the noise exhibits heavy-tailed behavior. In this paper, we investigate the convergence of vanilla Adam in both the expected risk and the empirical risk minimization, focusing on the effects of heavy-tailed noise and its relationship to index sampling. For the expected risk minimization, we establish convergence guarantees under Hölder smoothness and bounded $\mathfrak{p}$-th moment assumptions, allowing stochastic gradient noise with infinite variance. Our analysis provides explicit upper bounds on the expected squared gradient norm and shows that the iteration-dependent convergence term decays more slowly as $\mathfrak{p}$ decreases. For the empirical risk minimization, we establish asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and demonstrate that heavy-tailed population noise can deteriorate convergence bounds through dataset-dependent constants as the dataset size increases. Furthermore, under Lipschitz smoothness, we formulate multistage Adam with practical learning rate schedules and demonstrate that increasing batch sizes can reduce index-sampling noise and improve convergence guarantees and SFO complexity. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings on the effects of heavy-tailed noise and the computational benefits of increasing batch sizes.

item.title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
item.description: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.

item.title: A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling
item.description: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.

item.title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
item.description: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

item.title: When are dividend barriers optimal? A distributional characterization in renewal risk models
item.description: We study the finite-horizon optimal dividend problem in a renewal risk model with unrestricted dividend payments, examining how claim-size distributions determine barrier optimality. Under general assumptions on a fixed interclaim-time distribution, we prove that exponential claims admit a globally optimal barrier for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon. Conversely, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, every nonexponential law admits one fixed premium--discount pair for which no barrier is globally optimal at any sufficiently long horizon. These results establish, within this distribution class, an equivalence between exponentially distributed claims and the existence of a globally optimal barrier for every parameter combination in the stated range. Numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims with the same mean and illustrate how the claim-size distribution changes the structure of dividend decisions.

item.title: A Telescopic Method with Guaranteed B-Stationarity for Partitioned Cardinality and Complementarity Constraints
item.description: We consider the minimization of a smooth function subject to box constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints (PCC): the variables are divided into groups and, within each group, at most a prescribed number of variables may be non-zero. This class contains bound-constrained minimization, cardinality-constrained minimization and bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints. We introduce the Telescopic Method, which alternates iterations of a bound-constrained method on the faces of the feasible set with inexpensive one-dimensional "escaping" tests that exchange a variable of the current face by a currently null one within the same group. We prove, without constraint qualifications and without requiring global solutions of subproblems, that every limit point of the generated sequence is B-stationary, i.e., it satisfies the first-order condition defined by the tangent cone of the feasible set. This guarantee is obtained with exchanges of a single variable, whatever the number of non-null entries of the limit point, because B-stationarity for this class of problems decomposes into conditions on single variables. On the 60 bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints of the test set of Kirches, Larson, Leyffer and Manns, the method found approximately B-stationary points in all the problems. Applications to separable regression, sparse polynomial approximation and portfolio selection are described and tested numerically.

item.title: Consumption and Investment with Multiple Job-Switching Opportunities
item.description: We study finite-horizon optimal switching with affine rewards in a consumption-investment model with finitely many occupational regimes. Directed shortest-path costs yield the exact natural borrowing limit. A dual transformation reduces the control problem to a one-dimensional system of variational inequalities with interconnected obstacles. Convexity and a distributional waiting inequality give local spatial $C^{1,1}$ regularity and smooth fit, including destination ties. These estimates establish strong duality and recover optimal consumption, investment, and switching strategies. A reflected backward stochastic differential equation representation yields a set-based integral formula without prescribed boundary geometry. Every connected component of the spatially regular locus is a maximal smooth graph over time. Exact examples exhibit disconnected contact sets, temporal boundaries under strict triangle costs, and a corner in an individual boundary component under additive route costs. A convergent time discretisation completes the analysis.

item.title: Euler discretizations, invariant faces and brackets for lower exponents of positive switched systems
item.description: In this paper, we prove that explicit and implicit Euler discretizations yield monotone brackets for the lower Lyapunov exponent of positive switched systems. We establish convergence of the implicit bound for every Metzler family. For the explicit bound, we derive convergence criteria in reducible systems from a face formula for the uniform lower exponent on an invariant cone. The formula takes the minimum of the rates on faces that meet the cone nontrivially and are preserved by at least one mode, using only their preserving modes. For individually irreducible modes, we prove O(h) discretization errors, where h is the step size, and show that this order is sharp in general. At interior two-mode chattering optima with an irreducible optimal mixture, we obtain one-sided first-order bounds. We also construct a three-mode example in which the explicit bound converges while finite polytope lower bounds remain capped strictly below the true exponent. We prove convergence of fixed-antinorm Gripenberg brackets under individual irreducibility as the step and tolerance decrease and the search depth increases appropriately. Finally, we obtain independently verified continuous-time brackets by exact rational checks, with lower bounds that remain valid at smaller steps.

item.title: Quantum-Inspired Hamiltonian Descent for Radiation Therapy Treatment Planning
item.description: Direct incorporation of dose-volume constraints into inverse radiotherapy planning leads to large mixed-integer optimization problems that accurately represent clinical requirements but are computationally challenging. We develop and evaluate a quantum-inspired approach for automated dose-volume-constrained intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) and intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) planning. Clinical requirements are formulated as mixed-integer optimization problems, with binary variables representing dose-volume constraint violations. Patient-specific dose-influence matrices are generated at the photon control-point and proton spot levels, and intensities are optimized using Quantum-Inspired Hamiltonian Descent (QIHD). We evaluate QIHD on eight clinical cases: four IMRT (two prostate, one head-and-neck, and one liver) and four IMPT (two lung, one prostate, and one liver). The IMRT formulations contain 27,621 to 112,565 variables and are solved in 5 to 32 minutes, while the IMPT formulations contain 69,861 to 221,342 variables and are solved in 11 to 35 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU. QIHD produces dose distributions satisfying clinical protocols without manual intervention. In comparison, a CPU implementation of Gurobi fails to solve most tested mixed-integer formulations within several hours. These results demonstrate the computational feasibility of GPU-accelerated QIHD for automated photon and proton treatment planning. Prospective clinical validation and implementation of decomposed subproblems on quantum hardware remain future directions.

item.title: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
item.description: This paper establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (ERRL) framework for the continuous-time consumption-investment problem under a regime-switching market model with general utility functions. By incorporating randomized exploratory policies and Shannon entropy regularization into the stochastic optimal control formulation, we derive closed-form representations for the optimal exploratory consumption and investment strategies. Specifically, the optimal investment strategy follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, whereas the optimal consumption strategy takes the form of a Gibbs measure---which specializes to a Gamma distribution under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential distribution under power utility. Crucially, our theoretical analysis reveals that the classical deterministic optimal decisions correspond to the mode---rather than the mean---of these exploratory distributions. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the exploratory value function to its classical unregularized counterpart as the temperature parameter vanishes. For algorithmic design, we develop a continuous-time q-learning framework grounded in a novel continuous-time q-function, prove the policy improvement theorem, and establish martingale characterizations for both on-policy and off-policy learning. We find that parameterizing the actor network based on theoretical distribution families can help accelerate convergence and enhance numerical stability. Furthermore, numerical experiments across regime-switching environments provide empirical support for our theoretical findings, demonstrating stable loss convergence as well as the monotonicity and concavity of the learned value functions.

item.title: Finite-Time Tracking Success or Failure in the Pursuer--Evader Model
item.description: We investigate a sufficient framework for determining the success or failure of finite-time tracking in pursuer--evader dynamics. To this end, we design a nonsmooth coupled multi-agent system by adopting a previously established pursuer--evader model from the existing literature, which characterizes asymptotic tracking success and failure, as the backbone. We then provide appropriate sufficient conditions, expressed in terms of initial data, system parameters, and kernel functionals, under which some pursuers can successfully track evaders within a finite time, while others fail to do so. In particular, we show that the pursuer--evader subsystem associated with the pursuers that successfully track the evader, together with the corresponding evaders, exhibits finite-time stability.

item.title: Robust Optimization in Stochastic Games
item.description: A player's impatient valuation of an infinite stream of stage payoffs is a weighted average with nonincreasing weights. Such valuations generalize geometric discounting and allow imprecise or heterogeneous time preferences. For a stochastic game \(Γ\) and a profile \(u\) of impatient valuations, let \(Γ_u\) be the induced game. We ask when approximately optimal or equilibrium behavior can be chosen to vary continuously and stably with \(u\). We show that this robustness is governed by the corresponding uniform long-run payoff property: the uniform value in the adversary case, and uniform approximate equilibrium payoffs in the equilibrium case. In finite state spaces, the latter is equivalent to the usual existence of a uniform equilibrium payoff. In the two-player zero-sum case, if \(Γ\) has a uniform value, then the value of \(Γ_u\) varies uniformly continuously with \(u\), and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a uniformly continuous mapping assigning to each \(u\) an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal strategy in \(Γ_u\). Hence this holds for every finite two-player zero-sum stochastic game. In the non-zero-sum case, uniform approximate equilibrium payoffs imply a finite cover of the valuation-profile space by neighborhoods on each of which a single strategy profile is a robust \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium. For sunspot, correlated, and extensive-form correlated equilibria, uniform approximate equilibrium payoffs are equivalent to the existence, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), of a uniformly continuous mapping assigning to each valuation profile a robust \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium on a neighborhood of that profile. Consequently, every finite stochastic game admits uniformly continuous robust extensive-form correlated \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium selections.

item.title: Lower Bounds on Inference Complexity for Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent
item.description: In this paper, we establish sharp lower bounds for Gaussian approximation of Polyak-Ruppert averaged stochastic gradient descent with polynomially decreasing step sizes. For every fixed exponent $γ\in(1/2,1)$, a single one-dimensional smooth, strongly convex example has approximation error with the limiting variance of order $n^{1/2-γ}+n^{γ-1}$ in Kolmogorov and convex distances. This matches the existing upper bound throughout the range of $γ$. The nonlinear bias contributes $n^{1/2-γ}$ even when the Gaussian reference uses the finite linearized variance. We also derive a lower bound of order $n^{-(1-γ)/2}$ for the relative mean error of estimating the limiting variance from one SGD trajectory, uniformly over a scalar quadratic family. With the limiting variance known, achieving approximation error $\varepsilon$ on this example takes order $\varepsilon^{-4}$ iterations for the best choice $γ=3/4$. Achieving both Gaussian approximation and relative mean variance-estimation errors at most $\varepsilon$ uniformly over the model class requires at least order $\varepsilon^{-6}$ iterations for every fixed $γ$.

item.title: Adaptive Optimizers Can Get a Policy Ranking Wrong: Momentum, Dependent Data, and a Two-Run Remedy
item.description: Operators choosing among decision rules, such as when a battery charges or where an idle taxi goes, rank them by estimated long-run value. A standard estimator, linear temporal-difference (TD) learning, fits values from one stream of correlated observations. Large fits often use an adaptive optimizer, such as adaptive moment estimation (Adam), with fixed averaging rates. We show that these rates can change what is estimated, not just how fast: the same observations drive the updates and the optimizer's step-size scaling, moving the fit away from the intended TD value. The shift differs across rules, so it need not cancel in a comparison, and more data only makes a wrong ranking look more certain. Our remedy refits the same data at a second averaging rate that halves the effective gain, the number to which the leading shift is proportional. Twice the new fit minus the original removes that shift. In New York taxi and battery models calibrated to real data, common optimizer settings leave the selected rule unchanged but order close rules wrongly and misstate its value. Our remedy corrects nearly every wrong ordering, with one extra fit when the shift is moderate and two when it is larger.

item.title: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
item.description: We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $ε$-approximate Nash equilibria ($ε$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + ε$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $ε$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route. For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $ε$-NE, with matching instances for every $ε$. For small $ε$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $Θ(\sqrt{dε})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $Θ(hε)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $ε$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.

item.title: Entropic Column Generation and Lehmer Branch-and-Price for Bin Packing Problem
item.description: We introduce Lehmer branch-and-price, an exact algorithm for bin packing and cutting stock problems built on the Lehmer transform, the ratio of Mellin transforms of item weights at consecutive orders. The transform maps each bin, a finite multiset of item weights, to a smooth increasing curve, and so gives the discrete problem a continuous representation on which the tools of analysis, such as convexity, exponential families and smoothing, can act. Read along this curve, the problem yields an explicit dual solution, a monotone representation of the dominance order, a family of constructive heuristics with first fit decreasing as its limit, and an integer identity that tells when the linear relaxation can decide an instance and when only a perfect packing can improve the best solution known. Lifted from items to patterns, the transform gives entropic column generation, a new form of column generation that bounds the relaxation from both sides at every iteration without solving the pricing problem exactly, maximizes a smoothed dual at an explicit rate, and measures by an entropy how much the relaxation leaves undecided. We show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on the standard benchmark in both the number of instances solved and the computational time.

item.title: Singular Perturbations for Control Systems Safety
item.description: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) offer a powerful theory for enforcing safety in dynamical systems. Yet, applying this framework to complex systems is challenging when subsystems are feedback-interconnected and operate at different timescales. Such structures arise naturally in multiphysics systems and in control architectures where physical plants interact with optimization, estimation, and control algorithms. In many of these settings, safety involves only part of the system, motivating the design of reduced-order certificates. Inspired by singular perturbation theory, we establish sufficient conditions, involving separation between slow and fast dynamics, under which a reduced-order safety certificate can be lifted to the full interconnected system. Specifically, we construct a composite CBF ensuring forward invariance of a lifted subset of the original safe set. We also show that the certified safe set expands monotonically as the tuning parameter accelerating the fast dynamics is reduced. Numerical results validate the approach on two robotic systems: a planar 2-DoF manipulator with motor dynamics and a 6-DoF UR10e manipulator controlled by a suboptimal optimization algorithm.

item.title: Mixed-Integer Programming for Causal Discovery with Unknown Hard-Intervention Targets
item.description: When intervention targets are uncertain, learning causal relationships and identifying directly perturbed variables become a joint task. We develop an exact mixed-integer program based on optimized parent-set scores (PS-MIP) for joint graph and intervention-target estimation in linear Gaussian structural equation models under stochastic hard interventions. The method can incorporate candidate-edge restrictions and partial target knowledge when available. For each random variable, PS-MIP evaluates candidate sets of direct causes, or parent sets, by optimizing the likelihood parameters and compatible target patterns, retaining both the score and a minimizing target pattern. A global mixed-integer program then selects parent sets subject to acyclicity. Under stated conditions, this reduction preserves the joint objective and reconstructs the graph, targets, and likelihood parameters. Because the local scores are precomputed, PS-MIP replaces a direct large bilinear mixed-integer program with a linear selection problem; empirically it certifies global optimality on far more instances than the direct formulation (126 of 180 versus 34) and is often orders of magnitude faster. On synthetic data, PS-MIP achieves favorable false-discovery--true-discovery trade-offs relative to several benchmark algorithms for causal discovery with unknown intervention targets, along with strong intervention-target recovery in denser settings. An exploratory study on real data from a controlled physical system further demonstrates recovery beyond simulation.

item.title: Differentially Private Distributed Optimization via the Intrinsic Randomness of Zeroth-Order Estimators: Sampling Geometry, Convergence, and Privacy Guarantees
item.description: Distributed zeroth-order optimization has gained increasing attention in applications where exact gradients are computationally expensive or unavailable. However, the iterative exchange of local decision variables makes distributed networks vulnerable to inference attacks. While differential privacy provides a rigorous framework for privacy protection, conventional approaches generally require additional random noise, which inevitably affects optimization accuracy. In this paper, we investigate whether the randomness inherent in zeroth-order estimation can itself provide privacy protection. We develop a distributed zeroth-order gradient descent method that integrates consensus updates with a ball-uniform two-point gradient estimator. Our theoretical analysis shows that our algorithm attains standard convergence guarantees in both online and offline optimization settings. We then characterize the relevant probability distributions of the associated privacy mechanism, and establish differential privacy guarantees for both the online and offline optimization settings. These results reveal the potential of intrinsic zeroth-order randomness for privacy protection.

item.title: Benign population landscapes do not transfer to empirical risk minimization in nonsmooth optimization
item.description: Benign landscapes provide a geometric explanation for the success of iterative methods on nonconvex problems arising in data science. The landscape is benign if every local minimizer is global and every other critical point is a strict saddle. For methods that avoid strict saddles, convergence to a critical point therefore implies convergence to a global minimizer. For smooth stochastic optimization, a common strategy for establishing such landscapes proceeds in two steps: $(i)$ establish benign geometry for the population objective---which is often easier to analyze---and $(ii)$ transfer this geometry to the empirical objective using concentration of gradients and Hessians. Recent work has extended saddle-point avoidance guarantees to weakly convex nonsmooth optimization through the notion of active strict saddles. We show, however, that benign population geometry need not transfer to empirical objectives in this setting. Specifically, for robust phase retrieval with Gaussian measurements---a well-studied and highly structured problem---the population objective is benign. Nevertheless, the empirical objective has sharp spurious local minima with probability bounded away from zero as the sample size tends to infinity. This asymptotic probability lower bound is independent of the dimension.

item.title: Three-phase time minimization transportation problem with non-idle phases: a polynomial two-witness algorithm
item.description: The three-phase time minimization transportation problem partitions the origin-terminal links into three sets used in consecutive phases and minimizes the sum of the phase shipment times. Optimal solutions may leave a phase idle, as in the main example of the original study. We require every phase to carry a positive integer quantity while leaving the split of the total requirement across phases free. Discarding idle solutions from the original algorithm does not, in general, solve this variant. We prove that the optimum is attained by fixing one witness link in each of two phases and deciding the third phase by a single network flow computation, with the optimal Phase-3 time of each witness pair located by binary search. The resulting exact algorithm is strongly polynomial. It extends to any fixed number of phases, whereas, when the number of phases is part of the input, even non-idle feasibility is strongly NP-complete; feasibility alone is fixed-parameter tractable in the number of phases via known rainbow-matching results. We also characterize the minimum time of each phase. On the main example, non-idleness raises the optimum from 38 to 41. On 3,650 random instances with up to $50\times50$ links the algorithm took at most 50.2 seconds, and non-idleness raised the optimal value in 41% of the 2,250 instances with equal phase sizes; on 90 sampled instances it was faster than a mixed integer programming solver on 80 with a direct formulation and on 65 with a tighter threshold formulation.

item.title: Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
item.description: We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon. We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy. The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by s, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1-O(1/s) at every scale s >= 1 and every horizon T >= 1, so the ratio tends to 1 as s goes to infinity.

item.title: Dual Path Following for an Aerial Manipulator Under State and Input Constraints via Transverse Feedback Linearization
item.description: This paper studies dual path following for a quadrotor carrying a three-degree-of-freedom arm. The center of mass of the combined system must follow a vehicle path and the end effector must follow a second path, while the arm respects its joint limits and avoids its singular postures. The vehicle and the arm are mechanically coupled, so one controller must handle both paths. With the center of mass and the end-effector path coordinates as outputs, and a dynamic extension of the thrust, the system admits a normal form without internal dynamics. We characterize the states where this normal form fails. We formulate the transverse feedback linearizing controller as a quadratic program that relaxes only the speed of the end effector along its path and imposes safety and actuator limits as inequality constraints. The program reduces to a scalar problem with a closed-form solution. If it remains strictly feasible for all time, the feedback is locally Lipschitz, both paths are invariant and attractive, and every constraint holds. In the physics engine Drake, the controller resolves a conflict between the two speed references by slowing the end effector while both paths remain invariant. By contrast, a cascade with a safety filter leaves both paths. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/am_dual_pf-/

item.title: Robust Appointment Scheduling with Heterogeneous Costs
item.description: Designing simple appointment systems that under uncertainty in service times, try to achieve both high utilization of expensive medical equipment and personnel as well as short waiting time for patients, has long been an interesting and challenging problem in health care. We consider a robust version of the appointment scheduling problem, introduced by Mittal et al.\ (2014), with the goal of finding simple and easy-to-use algorithms. Previous work focused on the special case where per-unit costs due to under-utilization of equipment/personnel are homogeneous i.e., costs are linear and identical. We consider the heterogeneous case and devise an LP that has a simple closed-form solution. This solution yields the first constant-factor approximation for the problem. We also find special cases beyond homogeneous costs where the LP leads to closed form optimal schedules. Our approach and results extend more generally to convex piece-wise linear costs. For the case where the order of patients is changeable, we focus on linear costs and show that the problem is strongly NP-hard when the under-utilization costs are heterogeneous. For changeable order with homogeneous under-utilization costs, it was previously shown that an EPTAS exists. We instead find an extremely simple, ratio-based ordering that is 1.0604 approximate.

item.title: Long-time behavior of first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations in the Wasserstein space
item.description: We establish the long-time behavior of solutions $U$ to first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations in the Wasserstein space $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb T^d)$. For a class of Hamiltonians with quadratic growth, including non-convex ones, we prove that there exist a unique ergodic constant $λ$ and a solution $V$ of the associated ergodic problem such that $U(t,m)-λt$ converges to $V(m)$, uniformly on $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb T^d)$, as $t\to+\infty$. Finally, we provide applications to mean field control problems and zero-sum differential games.

item.title: Variance Reduction Note 3: The Convergence of PAGE
item.description: The probabilistic gradient estimator (PAGE) alternates randomly between an accurate gradient refresh and a cheap recursive correction. This third expository note on recursive variance reduction explains the algorithm and gives a self-contained convergence proof for smooth nonconvex optimization. A Lyapunov function combines objective decrease with estimation error, turning the refresh probability into an explicit contraction parameter. The resulting expected oracle complexity is $O(n+\sqrt n\,ε^{-2})$ for finite sums and $O(ε^{-3})$ for online problems, with the other problem parameters fixed. Initialization, refreshes, and both evaluations in each gradient difference are counted. The presentation is pedagogical and makes no claim of a new algorithm or convergence rate.

item.title: Learning Gradients of Homogeneous Functions
item.description: Homogeneous gradient functions have widespread significance, including applications in maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval problems. Euler's homogeneous function theorem specifies how the potential associated with a positively k-homogeneous gradient field can be recovered directly from the field itself. We use Euler's theorem to build on GradNets and propose a homogeneous gradient network architecture that is guaranteed to correspond to the gradient of a homogeneous function. Then, we describe how monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate the gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions. The inductive bias of homogeneous GradNets enables them to outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7dB in our max energy subspace projection experiment and by up to 13% higher accuracy, 98% fewer parameters, and 70% fewer FLOPS in our amortized inner product search experiment.

item.title: Strong convergence of a slowly damped primal-dual dynamical system with general time-scaling, Tikhonov regularization and implicit Hessian damping
item.description: This paper proposes a novel mixed-order inertial primal-dual dynamical system with general time-scaling and Tikhonov regularization coefficients, together with implicit Hessian damping, for solving convex optimization problems with linear equality constraints in Hilbert spaces. The proposed dynamical system incorporates slowly vanishing viscous damping and is developed based on a time-dependent Tikhonov-regularized Lagrangian. Under suitable assumptions, we establish fast convergence rates for the objective residual, the feasibility violation, and the primal-dual gap using a Lyapunov analysis. Moreover, we prove that the generated primal-dual trajectory converges strongly to the minimum-norm primal-dual solution. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and indicate improved convergence performance relative to the comparison dynamical systems.

item.title: Distributionally Robust Optimization over Incomparable Spaces
item.description: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provides a principled framework for making decisions under uncertainty when the underlying distribution may be incorrectly specified. A widely used approach builds on ideas from optimal transport (OT) as a means of measuring differences between distributions. However, this depends on these distributions residing in the same space. In certain settings, the reference data distribution we have and the space on which we make our decision may be different, which renders classical OT techniques impossible. In this paper, we provide a new DRO formulation in which ambiguity sets are defined through the Gromov-Wasserstein distance, which is an extension of OT to pairs of distributions residing in incomparable spaces. We show that several seemingly unrelated optimization formulations, including conditional value-at-risk minimization, group distributionally robust optimization, robust graph $k$-median, and $k$-median with outliers, can be recovered as special cases of our formulation. We describe the computational aspects of solving the proposed formulation based on the doubly-nonnegative relaxation. Last, we illustrate the framework through experiments on clustering over incomparable spaces and stochastic graph $k$-median.

item.title: Smoothed analysis of stability radii for the assignment problem
item.description: Every linear program can tolerate small changes to its costs and still yield a solution of the original problem. The size of this tolerance measures how robust an optimal decision is to noise or numerical error, and how much regularization the problem can support. Classical sensitivity analysis can determine this tolerance only from an optimal solution. This paper provides a priori lower bounds on two measures of this tolerance -- the optimality gap and the $\infty$-norm stability radius -- for the $n$-by-$n$ linear assignment problem over the Birkhoff polytope. The bounds derive from a smoothed analysis, which adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation of at least $σ$ in every direction to an arbitrary base cost. At every fixed confidence level, uniformly over the base cost, both quantities are at least of order $σ/(n\sqrt{\log n})$. The radius bound is asymptotically sharp. Under isotropic noise, the worst case occurs when every assignment has equal cost, and in this case, a scaled stability radius converges in distribution to a standard exponential variable.

item.title: Mean Field Game Problem with Kantorovich Potential Coupling: An Attrition model
item.description: In this work we address a class of Mean-Field Game (MFG) systems on the flat torus $\mathbb{T}^{d}$ in which individual agent incentives arise from macroscopic, distribution-dependent objectives governed by the Wasserstein-2 ($W_{2}$) distance. Taking the first variation (Lions derivative) of the Wasserstein-based macroscopic functional yields a coupled forward-backward system of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) and Fokker--Planck (FP) equations featuring a nonlocal coupling driven by the Kantorovich optimal transport potential. As a primary case study, we formulate a large-scale attacker-defender attrition model aimed at protecting High-Value Units (HVUs). By defining population-wise attrition rates via the $W_{2}$ metric and casting the defense strategy as a Pareto-optimal McKean--Vlasov control problem, we derive a concrete HJB--FP system with a Kantorovich potential coupling. We prove the local-in-time existence of classical solutions for this system using Schauder's fixed-point theorem. Finally, we compute the MFG dynamics by combining the Sinkhorn algorithm with ResNet-based Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and simulate two-dimensional attacker-defender engagements across diverse attrition parameters, control costs, and multi-HVU configurations.

item.title: OCP-Based Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Quadrotor Trajectory Tracking
item.description: Fast online optimization is essential for nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) on resource-limited aerial platforms. This paper presents an analytical-derivative NMPC solver for quadrotor trajectory tracking. For the state-affine translational model with held thrust and attitude commands, fourth-order Runge--Kutta integration yields an exact discrete-time prediction map. Forward--backward difference equations provide the gradient and exact Hessian of the finite-horizon cost condensed over the input sequence. These derivatives drive a nested optimal-control-based direction recursion, while a shifted warm start reuses the preceding solution. The resulting solver addresses the unconstrained tracking problem without a general-purpose nonlinear programming package. Gazebo experiments show comparable tracking accuracy to iLQR and two acados SQP configurations, with mean solver-time speedups of $1.97$--$2.30$. In onboard flight tests, the mean solver time is $0.3121$\,ms, corresponding to speedups of $3.37$--$5.77$ over the same baselines. The largest measured solver time is $3.7754$\,ms within a $20$-ms control period. These measurements cover the numerical solver and exclude estimation, communication, and command publication.

item.title: Long-Time Behavior of Zero-Noise Mean-Field Adam
item.description: Adaptive methods such as Adam are the most commonly used methods for training neural networks, but their long-time behavior is not as well understood as that of non-adaptive methods. This is particularly true in the mean-field limit, where the dynamics of infinitely many neurons are described as a distribution over parameters which satisfies a self-consistency condition. In this paper, we study a deterministic continuous-time model of Adam in the mean-field setting. Under a condition relating the averaging rates of the momentum and second-moment variables, the size of the gradients, and a regularization parameter, we prove that the distribution of parameters converges to the set of equilibria. This condition extends the range known for finite-dimensional models, and we show that it is sharp. Under an additional Lojasiewicz-type inequality for distributions, we prove that individual parameter trajectories converge and obtain quantitative rates for this convergence. We verify the qualitative convergence assumptions for a regularized two-layer neural network. We also show that adding noise to the momentum prevents the system from approaching these equilibria and rules out many free-energy type Lyapunov functionals. Finally, numerical experiments illustrate the energy estimates, give evidence of persistent oscillations outside the sufficient parameter range, and compare the observed decay with the predicted rates.

item.title: Multirate Data-Driven Predictive Control: Rank Obstructions, Identifiability, and Noise Conditioning
item.description: We develop rank, identifiability, and noise-conditioning results for compact input--output predictors in multirate data-driven predictive control. The inverse of a square zero-input response matrix used in an existing compact-lifting construction is shown to be undefined under its observability and minimal-polynomial assumptions. We derive exact replacements using rank-complete data, characterize all predictor extensions, and establish the minimum-norm and minimax Euclidean noise properties of the canonical Moore--Penrose extension. A joint predictor is identified directly from mixed experiments with arbitrary initial states. Deterministic perturbation bounds quantify reconstruction errors through informative singular-value margins, while a positive-definite reduced weighting preserves the nominal quadratic cost. Sampling-rate observability and event-triggering analyses identify additional conditions needed for reconstruction and stability guarantees.

item.title: Singular Tracking of Fractional Brownian Motion under Proportional Costs
item.description: We study adapted finite-variation tracking of fractional Brownian motion under quadratic loss and proportional adjustment costs. For $H\in(0,1)$, \[ V_λ(T;a,b,σ)\underset{λ\downarrow0}{\sim}κ_HT a^{(1-H)/(1+H)}(λb)^{2H/(1+H)}σ^{2/(1+H)}. \] The positive long-run cell value $κ_H$ is unchanged by full past information. A bounded full-past reset correction yields finite-horizon bounds and continuity in $H$. The Brownian value is $κ_{1/2}=\frac12(\frac32)^{2/3}$. Coupling local paths with their filtrations gives a local limit, which we verify for Gaussian Volterra targets. Every asymptotically optimal control has the same leading tracking--variation cost split. Primal and dual bounds quantify the cell value. For $H<1/2$, we construct a positive-factor approximation and relate factor resolution to horizon length.

item.title: Expected Minimax Regret Rates for Adaptive LQG Control on Fixed Parameter Sets
item.description: We study how a fixed model family determines expected minimax regret in adaptive LQG control. The family is compact and affine, with partial observation and unknown noise covariances. We quantify how information from residual covariances and input responses can vanish relative to differences between optimal control laws. This relation yields matching bounds that classify regret as bounded, logarithmic, sublinear polynomial or linear. Polynomial exponents are rational. For real algebraic model and cost data, a terminating procedure determines the regret class and the exact exponent of polynomial growth before data collection. A causal policy attains these rates using model estimation and bounded probes, reselecting model sets from observations without a supplied common stabilizer. For costs with fixed positive definite output and input weights, polynomial exponents are at most one half.

item.title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification
item.description: Convex regression provides a flexible nonparametric estimation framework while incorporating appropriate shape information. However, its standard least-squares formulation has $O(n^2)$ supporting-hyperplane constraints creating a computational bottleneck as the sample size $n$ increases. We study a $K$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) localized relaxation for convex regression where we for each sample, we only maintain the $K$ nearest hyperplane constraints. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish statistical guarantees for our modified estimator in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. In particular, for $d>4$, the population risk of our modified problem can be shown to have equivalent convergence rates as the original least square convex regression estimator of $\widetilde O(n^{-2/d})$ using neighborhoods sizes (i.e. $K=K_n$) of order $\widetilde O(n^{2(d-1)/(2d-1)})$ for general convex functions and $\widetilde O(n^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$ for strongly convex functions. To corroborate our theory, we implement iterative optimization methods to compare the prediction accuracy of the KNN relaxation with those of the full estimator across synthetic convex benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that KNN prediction risk approaches the full-estimator prediction risk at neighborhood sizes matching the theoretical scale.

item.title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
item.description: The Herfindahl--Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration, is widely used to quantify competitive balance in sports tournaments. To enable comparisons over time or across leagues, both its minimum and maximum should be known. The minimum is usually trivial. Our paper provides results on the maximum HHI in incomplete round-robin tournaments, where the set of matches is represented by a regular but not complete undirected graph. We prove that the lower bound of maximum HHI is reached when the tournament consists of independent round-robin groups, while the upper bound of maximum HHI is reached when the set of matches is represented by a bipartite graph. Maximising HHI is computationally difficult even for highly structured graph types corresponding to real-world tournaments, where the teams are partitioned into pots and play the same number of matches against opponents from every pot. The complexity of the problem does not depend on the scoring system or the number of opponents from a pot.

item.title: Optimization Frameworks & Learning Algorithms for Discrete-Time Mean Field Games
item.description: This monograph introduces discrete-time mean field games with finite state and action spaces, emphasizing optimization formulations and learning algorithms. Starting from Markov decision processes and finite-player stochastic games, it develops the notion of mean field Nash equilibrium, establishes existence and uniqueness results under suitable assumptions, and explains how mean field equilibria yield approximate equilibria in large finite-player games. Building on the linear programming formulation of Markov decision processes, occupation measures and primal-dual formulations connect equilibrium computation with mathematical optimization. The monograph presents fixed-point iterations, fictitious play, online mirror descent, and optimization-based methods, discussing their convergence properties and limitations. Numerical examples illustrate crowd motion, traffic routing, epidemic management, and the computation of multiple equilibria. It combines examples, theoretical results, and implementable algorithms, with bibliographic notes providing connections to the broader literature.

item.title: IncVNM: An Interactive Recommender System with Incremental von Neumann-Morgenstern Utility Learning
item.description: In modern recommender systems, users are often presented with products whose outcomes are random. The values of such products depend on their entire outcome distributions and on users' attitudes toward risk, making them difficult to evaluate using traditional product-level recommendation methods. We propose \textsc{IncVNM}, an interactive recommender system that incrementally learns a user-specific von Neumann--Morgenstern (VNM) utility function from ordinal click feedback generated during ordinary webpage browsing. At each interaction, \textsc{IncVNM} converts the click order within a displayed product list into pairwise comparisons between outcome distributions and updates the nominal utility by minimizing its deviation from the previous estimate while incorporating the newly observed pairwise comparisons. To close the interaction loop, an entropy-regularized sampling policy balances exploitation of the learned utility against exploration for additional preference information. We evaluate \textsc{IncVNM} in a rolling-window experiment with different response-error probabilities and show that it substantially outperforms the expected-return, mean--variance, discounted-UCB, and distribution-aware BPR baselines.

item.title: Multi-rate high-order regularization with an order-$(p-2)$ oracle
item.description:
We consider unconstrained minimization of a possibly nonconvex function $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ whose $p$th derivative is Lipschitz continuous, with $p\geq3$, when derivative information is available only through order $p-2$. The unavailable tensors $
abla^{p-1}f$ and $
abla^pf$ are reconstructed from central finite differences of $
abla^{p-2}f$. Since the two reconstructions have different point-query costs, we use a block length $m$ for the order-$p$ approximation and a subblock length $\ell\leq m$ for the order-$(p-1)$ approximation. The latter is transported between consecutive reconstruction points using the stored order-$p$ approximation. This leads to an adaptive regularization method that does not require prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant. We prove finite termination at an $ε$-approximate first-order stationary point and derive an explicit bound on the number of bundled order-$(p-2)$ oracle queries. For $m=(p-2)n^2$ and $\ell=(p-2)n$, the accuracy-dependent term has dimension--accuracy scaling $n^{3/p}ε^{-(p+1)/p}$. Thus the method retains the $ε^{-(p+1)/p}$ dependence of full order-$p$ regularization while using derivatives only through order $p-2$. Within the dense reconstruction framework considered here, using separate block and subblock lengths gives dimension dependence of order $n^{3/p}$, compared with $n^{4/p}$ when a common length is imposed.

item.title: On Exact Dual and Mixed-Integer Reformulations for Finite Horizon Markov Decision Processes with Submodular Revenue Maximization
item.description: We study exact mixed-integer reformulations of a finite horizon Markov decision process (MDP) with transition revenues defined by local submodular revenue maximization problems. We start with the dual linear programming formulation of the MDP, where local optimal revenues appear in the objective function and the constraints describe the state probabilities from the initial state. We combine the dual formulation with the binary variables of the local problems and obtain an exact mixed-integer nonlinear formulation with bilinear terms. We use the submodular inequalities and an exact McCormick linearization to obtain an equivalent mixed-integer linear formulation. We also use the dual structure to conduct a sensitivity analysis of the MDP optimal value with respect to changes in the local revenue coefficients. Based on local incumbent revenues and upper bounds, this sensitivity analysis evaluates the effect of local optimality gaps on the global MDP optimality gap, without solving every local revenue maximization problem to optimality.

item.title: Recent Developments in HPR Methods for Large-Scale Linear Programming
item.description: We present recent developments in Halpern Peaceman-Rachford (HPR) methods for solving large-scale linear programming problems. We first introduce the semi-proximal HPR framework and summarize its convergence guarantees, together with its connections to Halpern PDHG and ergodic Peaceman-Rachford iterations. To improve practical performance, we develop adaptive restart and penalty parameter update strategies. We then describe several computational enhancements, including GPU-based preprocessing, diagonal scaling, reusable execution plans for sparse matrix-vector multiplication, and sieving techniques. We further discuss multi-GPU parallelization and lossless model storage and loading for handling large-scale instances. These developments form the foundation of HPR-LP, a GPU-accelerated solver for large-scale linear programming.

item.title: Recent Developments in HPR Methods for Large-Scale Convex Composite Quadratic Programming
item.description: We present recent developments in Halpern Peaceman--Rachford (HPR) methods for solving large-scale convex composite quadratic programming problems. Within a unified HPR framework applied to the restricted Wolfe dual, we develop several algorithmic variants based on different choices of the semi-proximal operator $\mathcal{T}_1$ for the joint dual subproblem. Specifically, an sGS-based construction leads to a sequential $w$--$y$--$w$ update scheme, while a block-linearized construction eliminates cross-block coupling and enables parallel dual updates. To improve the latter, we further introduce a coupling-aware construction that exploits a second spectral moment to obtain a tighter row majorizer. We extend the framework to convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming through factor-based second-order cone reformulations. Additional computational enhancements include equality Gram scaling and asynchronous CPU polishing. We establish convergence results under fixed metrics and discuss practical adaptive strategies.

item.title: Convergence Guarantees for the Broximal Point Method under Perturbations
item.description: The Broximal Point Method (BPM) of Gruntkowska et al. (2025) comes with strong guarantees for convex optimization: under convexity alone, it terminates after finitely many steps and converges linearly in function value, with bounds that do not depend on the condition number or on any other regularity property of the objective. Each iteration, however, requires the exact minimization of the objective over a ball, which is generally intractable. As a first step toward implementable variants, we study the method when these subproblems are solved only approximately. We introduce and analyze Inexact BPM, which replaces the exact broximal point by an approximation and makes no assumption on how this approximation is obtained. Under summable or sufficiently small errors, we bound the number of iterations needed to reach a neighborhood of the set of minimizers, and these bounds remain independent of the regularity of the objective. Under the weaker requirement that the errors stay below the ball radius, we prove sublinear convergence in function value for the exact broximal points underlying the perturbed iterates, valid until the target neighborhood is reached, and we recover linear rates under bounded sublevel sets or strong convexity.

item.title: Multi-Period Donation Allocation for Food Banks under Stochastic Capacity and Supply
item.description: Each food bank within the national Feeding America network faces the challenge of distributing donated food equitably across the food-insecure population it serves while minimizing food storage and waste over a multi-period planning horizon. Donated food supply is highly stochastic, and distribution to beneficiaries is done by autonomous local agencies whose capacities are uncertain and vary over time. Based on our long-standing partnership with a regional food bank in the southeastern United States, we address the equitable and effective distribution of food donations to charitable agencies over a finite planning horizon under uncertain capacity and supply. We derive structural properties of this problem and use them to develop efficient heuristics. An extensive numerical study evaluates the performance of the heuristics relative to a stochastic dynamic programming benchmark, which suffers from the curse of dimensionality. One heuristic consistently provides near-optimal solutions and can be easily implemented by food banks. Our results also apply to other problems involving the equitable and effective distribution of scarce resources under stochastic capacity and supply.

item.title: OC-OPD: Observation-coordinated Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
item.description: Reverse and forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student's active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/OC-OPD.

item.title: Convergence properties of nonlinear RLC electrical networks
item.description: Convergence properties of general electrical networks with grounded nonlinear capacitors at the nodes and nonlinear inductors and resistors at the edges are studied. It is shown how, under appropriate conditions, for every initial condition there exists a unique equilibrium to which the system converges asymptotically. Partial extensions to networks with terminals or current sources are also provided. For RC networks this is compared with the use of an alternative storage function based on the co-content functions of the resistors.

item.title: Minimax-Optimal Static Estimators Under Interference
item.description: We study the problem of estimating the global treatment effect in randomized experiments under interference, where a unit's outcome may depend on the treatment assignments of other units. We adopt a minimax framework, allowing an adversary to select an outcome function from a class of functions that satisfy bounded outcomes and bounded interference. We derive minimax-optimal static estimators that are robust to a wide range of interference structures, parameterized by a scalar $δ$ controlling the maximum influence of one unit's treatment on another's outcome. Under large interference, we observe two regimes. When the treatment and control groups are equally sized, the minimax-optimal static estimator is the zero estimator. When one of the two groups is larger, the minimax-optimal static estimator is a "half-zero" estimator, in which the outcomes of the smaller group are ignored, and the estimator only considers the outcomes of the larger group.

item.title: Rare Event Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Large Deviations
item.description: We study finite-horizon reinforcement learning with a safety constraint on the probability of reaching a failure set. In contrast to the well-studied safe reinforcement learning literature, we consider problems where the probability of reaching the failure set is vanishingly small, but the consequences of reaching the failure set are catastrophic. Direct simulation and estimation of the optimal policy is naturally ineffective when the failure probability is extremely small. Moreover, on a real system the controller can only choose actions, and this is not enough to make failures frequent. In contrast to the rare event simulation literature, our goal is not to estimate the probability of the rare event occurrence, but to upper bound it such that the failure constraint is satisfied. Thus, instead of sampling failures, we use the large deviations principle. We define a damage variable that on exceeding a certain threshold indicates failure. We study the cumulant generating function (CGF) as its positive root provides an upper bound on the failure probability via Cramer's theorem. We extend this approach to Markov decision processes with hitting times through state-action CGFs, and give finite-horizon and state-dependent versions of the bound. The state-action CGFs do not depend on the policy and can be estimated from regular transitions, so the bound can be checked for any policy a priori. This gives a policy improvement algorithm in which every policy satisfies the failure constraint with high probability.

item.title: Adaptive Preference Elicitation in Preference Robust CPT-Based Shortfall
item.description: This paper investigates the cumulative prospect theory (CPT)-based shortfall risk measure where the value (utility) function and the distortion (probability weighting) functions are ambiguous. We propose a worst-case CPT-based shortfall risk measure where the capital requirement is based on the worst-case value function and distortion functions from an ambiguity set constructed with user-specific information (e.g., preference between risky and certain lotteries) and well-known general information such as the S-shape of the value functions. When the underlying random loss is discretely distributed and parameters in pairs of lotteries remain undetermined, we demonstrate that the worst-case value function and the distortion functions have a piecewise linear structure. Based on this observation, we develop an adaptive preference elicitation approach extended from the well-known polyhedral method to simultaneously elicit the distortion functions and the positive and negative parts of the value function by solving a sequence of mixed-integer linear programs. Based on the elicited distortions, we design new queries to construct a feasible set of the holistic value functions. The proposed framework iteratively shrinks the ambiguity set through designed queries, yielding a computationally implementable robust CPT-based shortfall risk measure. To examine the in-sample and out-of-sample performance of the elicited CPT-based preference functions and the resulting preference robust shortfall risk measure, we conduct numerical experiments under an S-shaped value function and inverse S-shaped distortion functions and report the corresponding results.

item.title: The local-to-global minimum problem of Calvert and Vamanamurthy: a quartic counterexample in three variables and the cubic case in all dimensions
item.description: In 1980 Calvert and Vamanamurthy asked whether a polynomial whose only critical point is a local minimum must attain its global minimum there. They gave counterexamples of every degree at least five in two or more variables and settled cubics in two and three variables and quartics in two variables, leaving open quartics in three or more variables and cubics in four or more variables. We resolve both remaining cases. First, we give an explicit quartic in three variables whose unique critical point is a nondegenerate strict local minimum, although the polynomial is unbounded below; the example extends to every dimension at least three, and its critical locus is a single point even over the complex numbers. Second, we prove that in every dimension a polynomial of exact degree three with a local minimum has another critical point, so that the cubic case holds vacuously; the proof is elementary and avoids the topological degree arguments used previously in two and three variables. Together with the results of Calvert and Vamanamurthy, this gives the complete classification of the local-to-global property by degree and dimension.

item.title: Split Cuts in Fixed Integer Dimensions
item.description: We study how many split cuts, which include the Gomory mixed-integer cuts, are needed to reach the integer hull, and how large split closures can be. In every fixed dimension, a rational pure-integer polytope admits a polynomial-time constructible split proof of its integer hull with polynomial total encoding length; consequently, its full split rank is polynomial in the input length. This establishes the split-rank conjecture of Basu, Conforti, Di Summa, and Jiang for bounded pure-integer polyhedra in fixed dimension. Central to our approach is a preservation result: in arbitrary pure-integer dimension, an inequality whose violating points map, under an integer-affine map, into the interior of a planar lattice-free polyhedron has a polynomial split proof retaining every point already satisfying it. Whereas Chvátal--Gomory closures have polynomial-size inequality descriptions in fixed dimension, split closures need not: tetrahedra of input length $Θ(\log N)$ can have split closures with at least $2N-1$ facets, yet extension complexity $Θ(\log N)$. For the two-row system $x=f+Rs$, $s\ge0$, $x\in\mathbb Z^2$ of input length $L$, the split closure has an exact extended formulation with $O(L)$ inequalities and auxiliary variables; this bound is tight. Separation over the split closure is polynomial-time in fixed total dimension. Finally, for mixed-integer feasible rational polytopes with fixed integer dimension $p$ and any continuous dimension, we maximize a primitive integral objective on the integer variables with $O_p(G+1)$ split cuts, each removing a current optimal LP vertex, until an optimal vertex is mixed-integer feasible; here $G$ is the integrality gap of the LP relaxation, rounded down.

item.title: Integrating Data Center Flexibility into Power System Operations: A Framework for Temporal Redispatch
item.description: Rapid growth in data center electricity demand, driven by artificial intelligence (AI) training and inference, is expected to increase stress conditions for power grids. Operational flexibility from data centers offers a near-term lever to relieve such stresses. Existing models of data center flexibility tend to bundle economic incentives with physical constraints, obscuring the tradeoff between economic willingness to shift load and technical limitations to do so. This paper proposes a temporal-redispatch focused framework that decouples data center demand flexibility into two independently parameterized dimensions: (1) systematic flexibility, capturing the economic environment through penalties for temporal shifting of data centers' scheduled demand, and (2) operational flexibility, capturing the physical envelope through the demand shifting time window and the limit on shifted data center demand. The framework relies on a direct current optimal power flow (DC-OPF) linear program which enables annual parametric analysis at hourly resolution. The framework is studied using a synthetic grid mimicking the Texas transmission system populated with the 2026 Adjusted Forecast from ERCOT (Electric Reliability Council of Texas). Results show that operational flexibility imposes a physical lower bound on unsatisfied demand that no economic incentive can overcome; longer shifting windows and higher limits on shifted data center demand reduce operational cost with different impacts on grid utilization; and, temporal redispatch shaves system-wide net load peaks while partially compensating for localized transmission bottlenecks that emerge under modeled coal retirement scenarios.

item.title: Overcoming Demand Censoring through Randomization for Risk-Sensitive Newsvendor Learning
item.description: We study online newsvendor learning with bounded demand, censored observations, and convex nonlinear shortage costs. Because stockouts can conceal the shortage magnitudes needed by gradient-based algorithms, we use randomized ordering to construct unbiased subgradient estimates. We characterize admissible randomization distributions within this framework and develop an online inventory policy that combines the resulting subgradient estimates with gradient-based updates. Our regret analysis quantifies the cost of randomization via the estimation variance and an additional loss term. We characterize the randomization distributions that minimize this objective. For piecewise-linear shortage costs, the optimal distribution is computed through a linear-time recursion; for costs with bounded curvature density, it is characterized by a scalar ordinary differential equation. The policy achieves expected regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed order in hindsight over $T$ periods. Under independent demand and suitable curvature of expected losses, the bound improves to $O(\sqrt{T})$. Matching minimax lower bounds establish rate optimality over the corresponding classes with a fixed marginal-cost bound. Both rates extend to nonperishable inventory under uniformly positive conditional expected demand. Numerical experiments on synthetic and retail data show improvements over alternative policies using censored observations.

item.title: Small-time controllability of affine systems and quadratic Lie brackets
item.description: We prove a new sufficient condition for small-time global exact controllability of finite-dimensional control-affine systems. It points out that, under a natural Lie algebra rank condition, quadratic Lie brackets are the only possible obstacles to controllability. This result extends to infinite-dimensional settings such as the global approximate controllability of diffeomorphisms. It also allows us to interpret recent results in PDE control theory.

item.title: Robust Closed-form Framework for Drag-Propulsive Control of Formation Flight
item.description: To conserve propellant, Distributed Space Systems (DSS) can leverage environmental forces to produce low cost relative forces, such as atmospheric drag in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). This work maximizes this strategy by developing robust, closed-form algorithms for optimal "hybrid" control, defined here as complementing the magnitude and directionality deficiencies of differential drag with the superior control authority of propulsive maneuvers within the same control window.
